blocks.text: 1. Mixed Precision Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445337691-462692430.png

Checkpointing, the previous topic, covered saving a network's progress to disk. Mixed Precision Training closes this module with a technique for speeding up training itself, rather than protecting it against interruption.
It works by using lower-precision numbers for most computations, without genuinely sacrificing accuracy, a genuinely clever practical technique explored in full depth throughout this topic.
2. A Quick Recap Of Numeric Precision

blocks.alt: A Quick Recap Of Numeric Precision
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445337691-467844032.png

A genuinely foundational computing concept underlies this entire topic. Numbers on a computer get stored using a fixed number of bits, like 32 or 16, determining how precisely a value can be represented.

More bits allow genuinely finer precision, but require genuinely more memory and computation, a fundamental tradeoff that Mixed Precision Training, already covered, directly exploits throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 3. The Full-Precision Default

This connects back to weights and activations, already covered throughout this course. By default, most deep learning computations use 32-bit floating point numbers, already covered in the previous section.
This is a genuinely safe, high-precision default that every earlier topic in this course has silently assumed, right up until this closing topic introduces a genuinely deliberate departure from it.
4. Mixed Precision Training's Core Idea
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445337691-754359812.png
Mixed Precision Training's genuinely core idea uses 16-bit floating point numbers for most operations, rather than the 32-bit default already covered in the previous section.

It reserves 32-bit precision only for the genuinely few operations that truly need it, giving this technique its own name: mixing two different precisions deliberately, rather than using just one throughout.
5. Why This Genuinely Speeds Things Up

blocks.alt: Why This Genuinely Speeds Things Up
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445337691-104061088.png

A genuinely real, practical hardware fact explains the benefit. Modern Graphics Processing Units can perform genuinely more 16-bit operations per second than 32-bit ones, a real, physical hardware characteristic.
Genuinely less memory used also allows genuinely larger batch sizes, already covered in its own topic, since each individual value now takes up only half the memory of the 32-bit default.
6. The Genuine Precision Risk
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445338602-640578922.png

This connects back to exploding and vanishing gradients, already covered in Gradient Clipping and Activation Functions. 16-bit numbers have a genuinely much smaller representable range than the 32-bit default.

Genuinely small gradient values can round down to exactly zero, losing information entirely, a genuinely real risk that the rest of this topic addresses directly through the technique covered in the next section.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: This precision risk, already covered in this topic, is not a hypothetical concern. It genuinely occurs in practice, which is exactly why loss scaling, covered in the very next section, became a standard, necessary companion technique.

blocks.text: 7. Loss Scaling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445338604-418535331.png

This connects back to the precision risk already covered in this topic. Loss scaling genuinely multiplies the loss by a large constant before the backward pass, already covered throughout the Backpropagation & Optimization module.

This keeps gradient values genuinely large enough to survive 16-bit precision, then divides back down before the update, a genuinely elegant, direct fix for the exact rounding-to-zero risk already covered in the previous section.
8. The Master Weights Copy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445338604-699023900.png

A genuinely important implementation detail follows. This connects back to Weight Decay's own small, cumulative updates, already covered in its own topic. A genuinely full-precision master copy of the weights gets kept.

This master copy gets updated by small 16-bit gradients, then rounded for use, preventing the genuinely tiny, repeated updates already covered as characteristic of Weight Decay from disappearing entirely under 16-bit rounding.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Mixed Precision Training Is Genuinely Valuable

Training genuinely large, computationally expensive networks, already covered in Network Architecture, is a direct case for Mixed Precision Training, since its speed and memory savings, already covered in this topic, become genuinely meaningful at that scale.

Running on hardware with genuinely specialized support for 16-bit computation is another genuine case; modern Graphics Processing Units are commonly built with exactly this kind of specialized support already covered earlier in this topic.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates the precision risk already covered in this topic, showing a genuinely small gradient value rounding to exactly zero under 16-bit precision, then surviving correctly with loss scaling applied.

code.content:
import numpy as np

small_gradient = np.array([0.00001], dtype=np.float32)
print("Original gradient (32-bit):", small_gradient)

# Simulating 16-bit precision loss by rounding to a coarser representable value
gradient_16bit_unscaled = np.float16(small_gradient)
print("Gradient cast to 16-bit, no scaling (already covered as the precision risk in this topic):", gradient_16bit_unscaled)

# Applying loss scaling, already covered in this topic
scale_factor = 1024.0
scaled_gradient = small_gradient * scale_factor
gradient_16bit_scaled = np.float16(scaled_gradient)
recovered_gradient = np.float32(gradient_16bit_scaled) / scale_factor
print("Gradient cast to 16-bit WITH loss scaling, then recovered:", recovered_gradient)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the unscaled gradient rounding to exactly zero under 16-bit precision, while the loss-scaled version survives and gets correctly recovered, exactly the fix already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Training Deep Networks: Module Complete

items: Mixed Precision Training uses lower-precision numbers for most computations to speed up training.
It uses 16-bit floating point for most operations, reserving 32-bit precision for a few operations that need it.
Modern Graphics Processing Units perform 16-bit operations faster and allow larger batch sizes due to lower memory use.
16-bit numbers have a smaller representable range, risking small gradient values rounding to exactly zero.
Loss scaling multiplies the loss before the backward pass, keeping gradients large enough to survive 16-bit precision.
A full-precision master copy of the weights preserves small, cumulative updates that 16-bit rounding would otherwise lose.
It is especially valuable for large, computationally expensive networks on hardware with specialized 16-bit support.
